source.title_on_document: Using Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation

paper_design_summary: The paper compares three pools of new-product ideas for college students priced at $50 or less: 200 ideas sampled from students in a 2021 product design course (before LLMs were available), 100 ideas generated by GPT-4 (gpt-4-0314) with zero-shot prompting, and 100 generated by GPT-4 with six example ideas (few-shot). No person received AI help. Prolific respondents rated each idea's purchase intent and novelty, and the authors computed pairwise cosine similarity of Google Universal Sentence Encoder embeddings within each pool.

studies.label: Student vs GPT-4 product-idea pools (the paper's Studies 1, 2, and 3 analyze the same 400 ideas)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned to people. The idea source (students in 2021, GPT-4 zero-shot, GPT-4 few-shot) defines the comparison. Only the presentation of ideas to raters was randomized: ideas were shown in random order, randomized at the idea level (p. 12, Section 5).
assignment.quote: For the student pool, we rely on data collected in 2021 in a product design and innovation course at an elite university.
assignment.locator: p. 10, Section 4 (Experimental setup); pools also described p. 3, Section 1

arms.name: Student ideas
arms.description: 200 ideas randomly selected from ideas generated by students in a 2021 product design and innovation course (title plus paragraph; average 63 words). Produced without AI.

arms.name: GPT-4 zero-shot
arms.description: 100 ideas generated by gpt-4-0314 (temperature 0.7) with the students' prompt, ten at a time, with compressed summaries of earlier ideas to avoid repeats; average 69 words. No person involved in production.

arms.name: GPT-4 few-shot
arms.description: 100 ideas generated by gpt-4-0314 with the same prompt plus six highly rated ideas from a separate student set; average 71 words. No person involved in production.

participants.exclusions: None stated. The 200 human ideas are a random sample of the course's ideas; the paper does not say how many of the 50 students contributed to that sample.
participants.who: Idea producers: students in a product design and innovation course at an elite university in 2021 (50 students in the course). Raters (not idea producers): college-age individuals from the United States recruited on Prolific; Appendix B reports N RespondentID = 200 in the purchase-intent model (p. 31) and 201 in the novelty model (p. 34). Each respondent rated about 40 ideas; each idea was rated about 20 times (p. 12).
participants.country: not_stated for students; raters from the United States (p. 12)
participants.quote: In this course, 50 students participated in an innovation challenge to come up with ideas for a physical product marketed to college students for $50 or less
participants.locator: p. 10, Section 4; raters p. 12, Section 5; Appendix B pp. 31, 34

ai_tool.how_used: The authors prompted GPT-4 directly to generate ideas (system prompt as a creative entrepreneur; ten ideas per request; zero-shot or with six example ideas). The AI output is compared with human output; no participant used AI.

task.description: Generate ideas for a physical product targeted at college students in the United States that could sell for less than about USD 50; each idea a title plus a 40-80 word paragraph.
task.duration: not_stated for students (innovation tournament in a one-semester course)

outcomes.name: Purchase intent (idea quality), Study 1
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Prolific respondents gave five-box purchase intent, weighted 0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00 (Jamieson and Bass 1989). Linear mixed-effects model with source fixed effects (humans baseline) and random intercepts and slopes for respondents and ideas. Robustness: alternative weights (Ulrich and Eppinger), idea-level simple regression on 400 ideas, cumulative link mixed model, ordered logistic regression, zero-shot baseline (Section 8.2.1, p. 23-24; Appendix B pp. 30-33).

contrasts.reported: Means: GPT-4 zero-shot 46.4% vs humans 40.4% (text, p. 13). Mixed model: beta = 0.059; 95% CI [0.031, 0.088]; t(246) = 4.06, p < 0.001 (p. 14). Appendix B: Source [Zero-Shot] 0.06, CI 0.03-0.09, p < 0.001; N RespondentID 200, N IdeaID 400, Observations 7982 (pp. 30-31). Simple regression: 0.256 points (95% CI [0.15, 0.37]; t = 4.602, p < 0.001); CLMM beta = 0.395; 95% CI [0.215, 0.575]; z = 4.31, p < 0.001 (p. 24).
contrasts.locator: p. 13, Figure 1 text; p. 14, Section 5; p. 24, Section 8.2.1; pp. 30-31, Appendix B
p. 13; p. 14, Section 5; p. 24, Section 8.2.1; p. 30, Appendix B

contrasts.reported: Two AI prompting conditions, no human producers: beta = 0.03; 95% CI [-0.01, 0.06]; t(199) = 1.892, p = 0.06 ('weakly significantly different'). Appendix B zero-shot baseline (unweighted scale): Source [Few-Shot] 0.12, CI -0.00-0.24, p = 0.058 (p. 32).

outcomes.name: Perceived novelty, Study 2 (Section 6.3)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Prolific respondents answered 'Relative to other products you have seen, how novel do you consider the idea for this new product?' on 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1. Linear mixed-effects model as for purchase intent. Robustness: idea-level simple regression, CLMM, ordered logistic regression, zero-shot baseline (p. 24-25; Appendix B pp. 33-36). Figure 3 notes say 'Novelty based on mTurk assessment', while the text says Prolific.

contrasts.reported: Average novelty: humans 40.6% (SD: 0.117) vs zero-shot GPT-4 36.7% (SD: 0.101) (p. 17); Figure 3 labels Mean 0.41 Std 0.117 vs Mean 0.366 Std 0.101 (p. 18). Mixed model: beta = -0.038; 95% CI [-0.066, -0.01]; t(269) = -2.67, p = 0.008 (p. 18). Appendix B: -0.04, CI -0.07 to -0.01, p = 0.008; N RespondentID 201, N IdeaID 400, Observations 8023 (pp. 33-34). Simple regression beta = -0.177; 95% CI [-0.286, -0.069]; t = -3.22, p < 0.0014; CLMM beta = -0.306; 95% CI [-0.514, -0.1]; z = -2.89, p < 0.01 (p. 25).

outcomes.name: Average pairwise cosine similarity within each idea pool, Study 2 (Section 6.1)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity of Google Universal Sentence Encoder embeddings, averaged over all pairs of ideas in a pool. Robustness: per-pool minimum spanning tree mean edge distance (512 dimensions, range 0 to 1): students 0.53, GPT-4 zero-shot 0.33, GPT-4 few-shot 0.3 (p. 24, Section 8.2.2). Sign reversed: higher similarity means less diverse.

contrasts.treatment_arm: GPT-4 (zero-shot and few-shot pooled; per-pool levels zero-shot 0.415, few-shot 0.428)
contrasts.reported: Average cosine similarity of all ideas: Student 0.221 (N ideas 200), GPT-4 zero-shot 0.415 (100), GPT-4 few-shot 0.428 (100) (Table 1). Two groups: eta^2 = 0.358, 95% CI [-0.197, -0.190], F(1, 24649) = 13715.82, p < 0.001. Three groups: eta^2 = 0.455, 95% CI [-0.210, -0.204], F(2, 29598) = 12340.95, p < 0.001. Direction coded for diversity (AI pools more similar, so less diverse).
contrasts.locator: p. 15, Table 1 and text; p. 16, Figure 2

contrasts.reported: Two AI prompting conditions: zero-shot GPT-4 ideas exhibit a significantly smaller cosine similarity than few-shot (eta^2 = 0.004, 95% CI [-0.018, -0.010], F(1, 9898) = 44.24, p < 0.001); 0.415 vs 0.428 (Table 1).

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine similarity within pool (MST mean edge distance as robustness)
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of ideas within each pool (human pool mixes ideas from different students; AI pools come from one model)
diversity_detail.uncertainty: One-way ANOVA over pairwise similarities (F tests with pair-level degrees of freedom); no adjustment for non-independence of pairs
diversity_detail.notes: No person used AI; this compares a pool of AI ideas with a pool of human ideas. Pair counts are not printed; the F statistics' degrees of freedom are as printed.

outcomes.name: Fraction of overlapping ideas (cosine similarity > 0.8) and estimated number of discoverable ideas, Study 2 (Sections 6.1-6.2)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: An idea counts as overlapping if its USE cosine similarity to a previously added idea exceeds 0.8 (text, pp. 8, 14); Table 1 notes instead define the fraction using an idea's average pairwise similarity to all other ideas. Capture-recapture model (Kornish and Ulrich 2011) converts overlap into T, the estimated number of discoverable ideas. Thresholds 0.7, 0.75, 0.85 as robustness (p. 24). The paper labels this 'flexibility'.

contrasts.reported: Fraction with cosine similarity > 0.8: Student 0, GPT-4 zero-shot 0.05 (Table 1). Binomial test: human fraction 95% CI [0.0, 0.0184]; RD = -0.05, 95% CI [-0.093, -0.007], p < 0.001 (p. 15). 5 of 100 zero-shot ideas overlapping; u(100) = 0.95; T = 966 ideas; human ideas all unique (p. 17). Thresholds: 0.7 gives 25, 0.75 gives 16, 0.85 gives 2 overlapping zero-shot ideas (p. 24).
contrasts.locator: p. 15, Table 1 and text; p. 17, Section 6.2; p. 24, Section 8.2.2

contrasts.reported: Fraction > 0.8: Student 0, GPT-4 few-shot 0.07 (Table 1). RD = -0.07, 95% CI [-0.120, -0.020], p < 0.001 (p. 15). 7 of 100 few-shot ideas redundant; u(100) = 0.93; T = 680 ideas (p. 17). Thresholds: 0.7 gives 37, 0.75 gives 23, 0.85 gives 1 overlapping few-shot ideas (p. 24).
contrasts.locator: p. 15, Table 1 and text; p. 17; p. 24

contrasts.reported: Difference between the two GPT-4 pools: RD = -0.02, 95% CI [-0.086, 0.046], p = 0.56.

diversity_detail.metric: Share of ideas whose USE cosine similarity exceeds 0.8 (overlap), and capture-recapture estimate of total discoverable ideas
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each idea against the ideas previously added to its pool (text); Table 1 notes say each idea's average pairwise similarity to all other ideas in the pool
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Binomial test on the fraction of overlapping ideas (risk differences with 95% CI); none for T
diversity_detail.notes: The paper calls this flexibility; coded as diversity because it compares outputs across the pool, which for students mixes different people's ideas. AI pools come from one model.

outcomes.name: Share of the top decile of pooled ideas by purchase intent, Study 3
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Ideas ranked by mean purchase intent; top 40 of 400 (top 10%) listed in Table 2. Robustness: top 5% and top 15% (Table 4, p. 25).

contrasts.reported: Fraction of the top decile from source: Student 5/40, GPT-4 zero-shot 15/40, GPT-4 few-shot 20/40; average quality of top decile 0.62, 0.64, 0.66; average novelty of top decile 0.45, 0.35, 0.33 (Table 3). 35 of 40 (87.5%) from GPT-4; chi-square vs equal representation (20, 10, 10): x^2 = 26.39, p < 0.001, df = 2 (p. 20). Top 5%: 1/20, 6/20, 14/20 (quality 0.64, 0.67, 0.68); top 15%: 11/60, 22/60, 27/60 (quality 0.60, 0.62, 0.64) (Table 4).
contrasts.locator: p. 19, Table 2; p. 20, Table 3 and text; p. 25, Table 4

outcomes.name: Quantile regression of idea-level mean rating on AI source, Study 3
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Quantiles 0.1 to 0.9 of MeanRating ~ SourceAI (GPT-4 zero-shot and few-shot pooled = 1, student = 0). Intercepts (1 to 2.18) indicate a rating scale other than the 0-1 purchase probability; the paper does not say which.

contrasts.locator: p. 21, Figure 4; p. 30, Appendix A, Table A.1

company_involvement.description: Funding from the Mack Institute for Innovation Management at the Wharton School; no company involvement stated. GPT-4 accessed from OpenAI as a tool.

eligibility.reason: No person received AI assistance: the paper compares ideas written by students in 2021 with ideas GPT-4 generated on its own (p. 3, p. 10). Criterion 2 does not apply; the course had 50 students, and the paper does not say how many contributed to the 200 sampled ideas. Ratings and embeddings score the ideas themselves.

one_line_finding: GPT-4 ideas had higher mean purchase intent than student ideas (46.4% zero-shot and 49.3% few-shot vs 40.4%, p. 13-14) but lower rated novelty (36.7% and 36.1% vs 40.6%, p. 17-18) and higher average pairwise cosine similarity (0.415 and 0.428 vs 0.221, Table 1, p. 15); no person used AI.
open_questions: Figure 1 (purchase intent, p. 13) is annotated Mean 0.41 / 0.366 / 0.361 with Std 0.117 / 0.101 / 0.111, identical to the novelty Figure 3 (p. 18), while the text on p. 13 gives purchase intent 40.4%, 46.4%, 49.3%. The figure labels may be copied from the novelty figure.
The introduction (p. 3) gives average purchase intent 0.48 for AI vs 0.40 for humans and perceived novelty 0.36 vs 0.41; these pooled AI numbers do not appear elsewhere.
Table 1 notes (p. 15) define the overlap fraction by each idea's average pairwise similarity, while the text (pp. 8, 14) defines overlap against any previously added idea.
The document title and author order differ from the search record ('Ideas Are Dimes a Dozen', Girotra et al. 2023, SSRN 4526071). Confirm that this file is the latest version of that record.
notes: The paper labels its analyses Study 1 (purchase intent), Study 2 (similarity, overlap, novelty), and Study 3 (top ideas); all use the same 400 ideas, so the form records one study. The 'treatment' arm in each contrast is the AI pool and the 'control' is the student pool. GPT-4 few-shot vs zero-shot contrasts compare two AI prompting conditions and are coded 'other'. Ideas were shown to raters in random order (p. 12); that is the only randomization. IRB: University of Pennsylvania, Protocol #853634, May 2023 (p. 12). Raters took the survey in May and June 2023 (p. 23). Page numbers are PDF page indices (the document prints none).
